blocks.text: In 1H NMR the sample is dissolved in an excess of solvent. Ordinary solvents contain hydrogen atoms, which would give strong signals that interfere with the spectrum of the sample: if ordinary CHCl3 were used, the signal of its single proton would be large enough to swamp the weaker signals of the sample. Deuterated solvents such as CDCl3 (deuterated chloroform) or CD3OD (deuterated methanol) are therefore used. In CDCl3 the hydrogen is replaced by its isotope deuterium (D), which needs a different radio frequency to flip, so it neither absorbs the radio waves used nor gives a peak in the 1H spectrum. The solvent is 'silent' and only the sample's signals are seen.

blocks.prompt: Why is CDCl3 used instead of CHCl3 as the solvent for 1H NMR?
blocks.explanation: Deuterium does not absorb at the proton frequency, so CDCl3 gives no peak to hide the sample's signals; CHCl3's large proton signal would mask them.

items: Deuterated solvents (CDCl3, CD3OD) give no 1H signal: the solvent is 'silent'.
